case.say: Alright, this is Module nine, the integrated case. There's no new theory here. Instead, you apply Modules one through eight to one family, the Calloways, an original practice case with twenty-two linked decisions. First, read the whole case slowly and take notes. Flag the contextual variables: age, marital status, children, net worth, income, and any special circumstances. And here's a useful tell: when a topic is raised and then expanded later in the case, expect a question on it. Answer the easy questions first and park the long calculations. Then for each question, read the last line first so you know what's being asked. Answer the rule-only questions straight away, eliminate impossible choices, and go back into the case only for the fact-specific ones. At the end, check that every question is answered, then review. Before you recommend anything, the planner reviews goals and time horizon, risk tolerance, the tax situation, liquidity and marketability needs, and the balance sheet and cash flow statement. If goals are unrealistic for the resources, you revise them, and fairly certain resources like a bonus or inheritance may be counted. Now the exam trap, and it's a big one in case work: case questions are loaded with facts that belong to a different question. Before calculating, write down the two or three facts the question really needs. For example, T-bill interest needs the federal rate only, not the state rate. With a client, you'd say: before I recommend anything, I need the whole picture, your balance sheet, cash flow, taxes, goals, and how you feel about risk, because every recommendation has to fit all of those at once.

Here's the family. Graham Calloway is fifty-three, an operations director at a private freight company, earning one hundred sixty-five thousand. Nadia is fifty, a software engineer at Kestrel Diagnostics, a public company, earning one hundred eighty-five thousand. They're married filing jointly and they itemize. Leah is fifteen and starts college in three years; Sam is eleven. Insurance is adequate. Net worth is about two point zero five million. Investment assets are about one point four five million, and Kestrel stock, four thousand shares at ninety dollars, is three hundred sixty thousand of that, nearly a quarter, with a basis of just forty dollars a share. Living expenses run thirteen thousand five hundred a month, and they have a forty-seven thousand six hundred dollar annual surplus. Their goals: a six-month cash reserve, Leah's first-year college money in three years, retirement in about twelve years, less reliance on Kestrel without a big immediate tax bill, and low costs and taxes. Their joint questionnaire says moderate. But Graham sold most of his stock funds near the bottom of a past bear market and says a fifteen percent drop would cost him sleep, and he wants low-cost index funds. Nadia is comfortable with volatility and wants an active sleeve in emerging markets and REITs. Planning assumptions: three percent inflation, a four percent T-bill rate, a ten percent market return, a thirty-two percent federal and five percent state bracket, Kestrel's beta of one point four with an eleven percent expected return, and a six and a half percent return needed for retirement. Nadia isn't an insider. Flag those contextual variables now; nearly every one drives a question later.

Decision one is the investment policy statement. The IPS sets objectives, the allocation policy, management procedures and communication, and its core content covers return requirement, risk tolerance, liquidity, time horizon, legal and regulatory factors, taxes, unique circumstances, and permitted or excluded investments. Question one asks where the six-month reserve and Leah's tuition in three years belong. Those are known cash needs the clients must be able to reach, so they go in the Liquidity section. Question two is the heart of it, risk tolerance, which has two dimensions. Ability to take risk comes from resources and circumstances. The Calloways have about two million dollars of net worth, two incomes, good insurance, and a twelve-year horizon, so their ability is high. Willingness is emotional comfort, and Graham panic-sold in a past bear market and fears a fifteen percent drop, so willingness is low. The IPS records both, then tests whether the risk level they'll accept can earn the six and a half percent they need. If it can't, you discuss taking more risk, lowering the goal, or both. The quick tell: a number or a resource speaks to ability; a reaction or feeling speaks to willingness. The common wrong methods are treating the questionnaire score as the whole answer and filing near-term cash needs under the return requirement. The exam trap: a rich client is not automatically an aggressive one, and the IPS must address both dimensions. With a client, you'd say: your finances could ride out a rough market, but if a drop would make you sell, the plan has to account for that, or we lower the target together.

Decision two is the cash reserve and how to react when things change. A reserve held in liquid form lets clients absorb setbacks without selling long-term assets or borrowing, so safety and access matter more than yield. Question three: the target is six months times thirteen thousand five hundred, or eighty-one thousand. Liquid assets total sixty-two thousand. The gap is nineteen thousand, added to a money market holding from the surplus or taxable assets. Question four: the money market mutual fund is not federally insured; a bank money market deposit account is, up to two hundred fifty thousand per ownership category. Question five is the real return on T-bills. Four percent times one minus thirty-two percent is two point seven two percent after tax, with no state tax because T-bills are state-exempt. Then divide, don't subtract, for inflation: one point zero two seven two over one point zero three, minus one, is negative zero point two seven percent. Question six: stocks fall twenty-five percent, but jobs, goals and reserves are intact, so you stay the course, hold the IPS allocation, and remind Graham why it was chosen. Question seven sorts change. A raise is incremental, and a one-week dip is noise. Nadia's layoff is discontinuous, so you revisit the IPS. The answer is three only. The exam trap: when a client insists on moving to cash in a downturn, the textbook answer is usually to maintain the allocation. With a client, you'd say: your reserve is there so you never have to sell stocks in a bad market, and today's drop doesn't change your goals, but a job loss would.

Decision three has two problems: the long-term mix, and a stock that's a quarter of investment assets and three quarters of the taxable equity sleeve. Question eight: Graham wants passive and low cost, Nadia wants an active emerging markets and REIT sleeve. Core and satellite satisfies both, a passive index core plus a smaller active satellite. Question nine: diversify Kestrel without an immediate tax bill and keep the value in the family. That's an exchange fund, where you contribute the stock for a share of a diversified pool. Selling outright would tax the two hundred thousand dollar gain. Question ten is a protective put: forty puts at an eighty dollar strike, two fifty premium. The premium is ten thousand. The floor is four thousand shares times eighty, three hundred twenty thousand, and net of premium it's three hundred ten thousand. Question eleven: a no-cost floor at eighty, giving up upside above one oh five, is a zero-cost collar, buy the eighty puts and write the one oh five calls. Question twelve is CAPM. The market risk premium is ten minus four, six percent. Times a beta of one point four is eight point four. Add the four percent risk-free rate and Kestrel needs twelve point four percent. Analysts expect only eleven, so it plots below the security market line: don't add. The exam trap: a covered call is not a crash hedge; it only cushions the drop by the premium received. With a client, you'd say: a quarter of your investments ride on the company that also pays your salary, so let's spread that risk without a big tax bill and set a floor while we do it.

Decision four is about risk measures. Beta is only meaningful when the holding is diversified and R squared is high. Question thirteen is the weighted beta of the taxable stock holdings. Multiply each value by its beta: Kestrel gives five hundred four thousand, Harborline ninety-seven thousand seven fifty, Summit thirty-three thousand three fifty-four. That sums to six hundred thirty-five thousand one hundred four. Divide by the total value of four hundred eighty-two thousand sixty and the portfolio beta is one point three two. Question fourteen asks which fund would diversify an index holding. Square each correlation to get R squared, and only the International Developed Index, at zero point three eight, falls below the zero point seven cutoff. Question fifteen compares Alder and Bexley. Bexley's R squared is only zero point five eight, so its beta, and its Treynor ratio, are unreliable. Use Sharpe, which uses total risk. Alder's excess return of seven point six over a standard deviation of sixteen, zero point four eight. Bexley's is nine over twenty-two, zero point four one. Alder wins, even though Bexley's raw return was higher. Question sixteen looks at Harborline: a one point two five percent expense ratio, one hundred forty percent turnover, and a departed manager. Turnover costs sit outside the expense ratio, high turnover can mean taxable gains distributions, and a manager change means monitor closely. The answer is one, two, and four. The exam trap: last year's top ranking is not a reason to pick a fund. With a client, you'd say: Bexley earned more, but it took much bigger swings to do it, and per unit of risk Alder did better.

case.at: Taxes: wash sales, TEY and placement
case.say: Decision five brings three tax tools: avoid wash sales, compare munis on a taxable-equivalent basis, and put tax-inefficient holdings in tax-deferred accounts. Question seventeen. The Calloways sold Harborline for eighty-five thousand against a hundred thousand basis, a fifteen thousand dollar loss, then bought it back twenty-one days later for eighty-two thousand. That's within thirty days, so it's a wash sale. The recognized loss is zero, but it isn't gone. It's added to the new basis, so eighty-two plus fifteen gives a basis of ninety-seven thousand. Don't treat the loss as lost forever, and don't apply the three thousand dollar capital loss limit here. Question eighteen. A double-exempt muni fund yields three point six percent versus a five point two percent corporate fund, with a thirty-two percent federal and five percent state bracket, and they itemize. For an itemizer, multiply the two complements: zero point nine five times zero point six eight is zero point six four six. Three point six divided by that is five point five seven percent, which beats five point two, so the muni wins. The wrong answers are five point two nine using federal only, and five point seven one from adding the brackets, which is the non-itemizer method. Question nineteen is placement. Taxable bond exposure goes in the four oh one k, and tax-efficient index funds or munis go in the joint account. The exam trap: Treasury interest is state-exempt, while muni interest is federal-exempt and state-exempt only in-state. With a client, you'd say: that three point six percent tax-free fund is worth about five point six taxable for you, so it beats the bond fund.

case.at: Bond risk and the college money
case.say: Decision six is about bond risk, and Leah's college money. Duration measures how sensitive a bond's price is to rates, and it should line up with the goal's time horizon. A bond fund never matures, so you can't hold its price risk away. Question twenty. The Ridgeway fund holds sixty thousand dollars, with a duration of six point two and a yield to maturity of five point two percent, and rates rise one percent. The price change is negative duration times the rate change divided by one plus the yield. Zero point zero one divided by one point zero five two is about zero point zero zero nine five. Times six point two is a drop of about five point eight nine percent, leaving roughly fifty-six thousand four hundred sixty-four dollars. Question twenty-one. Leah's ninety-six thousand dollars sits in stocks, and tuition is due in three years. Money needed within five years should generally leave stocks. The fix is immunization, matching duration to the horizon, so price risk and reinvestment risk offset. A three-year Treasury zero has a duration of exactly three, with no default or reinvestment risk. One caution: in a taxable account, a zero's accrued interest is taxed each year as phantom income. The wrong moves are reaching for yield with a long-duration fund, or using a barbell for a dated goal. The exam trap: in the duration formula, y is the current yield to maturity, not the coupon rate. With a client, you'd say: Leah's money has a due date, so we buy something that comes due on that date, and then rate moves and market drops can't change what she gets.

Decision seven, the last one, is currency. A foreign holding's dollar return combines its local return with the currency move. The easiest way to think about it: the money travels abroad when you buy and comes home when you sell. Question twenty-two. The Calloways invested thirty-six thousand dollars in the Summit European fund when one euro cost one dollar and eight cents. So they bought about thirty-three thousand three hundred thirty-three euros. The fund rose nine percent in euros, to about thirty-six thousand three hundred thirty-three euros. But now a euro buys only one dollar and two cents, so bringing the money home gives thirty-seven thousand sixty dollars. That's a gain of one thousand sixty on thirty-six thousand, about two point nine four percent. The shortcut is one point zero nine times one point zero two over one point zero eight, minus one. The wrong answers are reporting nine percent, the local return only, subtracting the currency loss, or inverting the exchange rate. For practice, if the euro had instead risen to one dollar twelve, the dollar return would have been about thirteen percent. The exam trap: a U.S. investor in foreign securities wants the dollar to fall during the holding period, because a stronger dollar shrinks the return when the money comes home. With a client, you'd say: your European fund did well in euros, but the euro lost ground to the dollar, so you kept about three percent of that nine, and that currency swing is part of the diversification you're buying.

Finally, the answer map, all twenty-two questions in one place, each tied to its learning objective and textbook page. Questions one through seven are the IPS and reserves: Liquidity; high ability but low willingness reconciled with the six and a half percent need; a nineteen thousand dollar reserve gap; the money market fund isn't insured but a bank deposit account is; a negative zero point two seven percent real T-bill return; stay the course; and three only, the layoff. Questions eight through twelve handle the allocation and Kestrel: core and satellite, an exchange fund, a three hundred ten thousand dollar net floor, the zero-cost collar, and a twelve point four percent required return, so don't add. Questions thirteen through sixteen are risk measures: a one point three two beta, the International Developed Index at zero point three eight R squared, Alder on Sharpe, and one, two and four for Harborline. Questions seventeen through nineteen are taxes: a zero loss with a ninety-seven thousand basis, a five point five seven percent TEY favoring the muni, and taxable bonds in the four oh one k. Then bonds: about fifty-six thousand four hundred sixty-four after the rate rise, and three-year Treasury zeros for Leah. And the currency question: two point nine four percent. The pattern to take into the exam is that one family's facts feed every module, and the skill is pulling the two or three facts each question needs. With a client, you'd tie it together like this: every piece of your plan, the reserve, the mix, the Kestrel stock, taxes, and Leah's college money, has to fit together, and that's what we just built.
